div.p: Advancements in compositional real-time scheduling frameworks have made it feasible to build large and complex real-time systems by composing multiple subsystems also known as components. Different frameworks with different resource models have recently been proposed for a variety of realtime task models. However, these works have focused their analysis on efficient scheduling of components' task set under a given resource model, providing little or no interest on energy consumption, which has become an important issue in many recent real-time embedded applications. In this paper, we propose a new compositional scheduling framework to compose multiple power-aware components. We introduce the power-aware periodic resource model, and the power-aware interface model to abstract the real-time and energy requirements of a component in the system. The schedulability analysis of the framework is provided under both EDF (Earliest Deadline First) and RM (Rate Monotonic) scheduling policies.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recent advancements in compositional or hierarchical realtime scheduling frameworks have made it feasible to build large and complex real-time systems by composing multiple subsystems also known as components. Component-based design provides a means for decomposing a system into components, allowing the reduction of a single complex design problem to multiple simpler design problems, and composing components into a system through component interfaces that abstract and hide their internal complexity. Component-based design also facilitates the reuse of components that may have been developed in different environments. Different frameworks [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [7] with different resource models have therefore been proposed for a variety of real-time task models.

However, current researches on compositional real-time scheduling frameworks have focused their analysis on efficient scheduling of components' task set under a given resource model, providing little or no interest on energy consumption, which has become an important issue in many recent embedded real-time applications. Many techniques [10], [11], [12], [14], [13], [8] have been suggested to reduce the energy consumption of real-time constrained tasks. One of the common techniques for reducing dynamic energy consumption is based on the Dynamic Voltage Frequency Scaling (DVFS) scheme which dynamically scales the processor frequency. Existing DVFS techniques can be classified into static schemes [14] that determine the optimal processor speed level offline, and dynamic schemes [10], [11], [12], [13], [8] that utilize unused slack times at run-time to adjust the processor speed without violating tasks deadlines.

However, to the best of our knowledge, little work has been done on power-aware scheduling in compositional realtime scheduling framework. In this paper, we consider the periodic real-time task model and propose a new compositional scheduling framework to compose multiple power-aware components. We introduce the power-aware periodic resource model Γ(Π, Θ, Ψ) to provide exactly Θ computational time units every period Π with the processor speed set to Ψ, and the power-aware interface model to abstract the real-time and energy requirements of a component in the system. The schedulability analysis of the framework is provided under both EDF (Earliest Deadline First) and RM (Rate Monotonic) scheduling policies.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the proposed power-aware hierarchical real-time scheduling framework, including the power-aware periodic resource model and interface model. The schedulability of the framework is analyzed in Section III, while the conclusion comes in Section IV.

div.head: II. POWER-AWARE HIERARCHICAL REAL-TIME SCHEDULING FRAMEWORK
div.p: In this section, we propose a new compositional scheduling framework to support power-aware real-time systems. We therefore define new resource and interface model for the framework.

div.head: A. Energy and Task Model
div.p: In this paper, we consider a compositional real-time scheduling framework running on a single processor system. We assume the processor to be equipped with dynamic voltage frequency scaling (DVFS) mechanism allowing it to continuously adjust its operating frequency. Let us consider an application with execution time t running on a processor with maximum frequency f max . If the processor runs at frequency level f (0 < f ≤ f max ), the relative processor level is given by f /f max . Thus, the application execution time on the processor with speed level s is defined by t/s, where t is the execution time with the maximum processor speed level. That is, the application execution time is slowed down by a factor of s. The power consumption of the application is generally in proportion to t and s 3 .

The basic unit of scheduling in compositional or hierarchical scheduling framework is called a scheduling component and defined as a triple of C(W, R, A), where W is the workload in the component, R is the resource model specifying the resource allocations available to the component, and A is the scheduling algorithm inside the component [4].
A component workload W consists of n periodic tasks. Each task is represented by four tuples, τ i = (p i , e i , f i , g i ).

Task τ i releases an instance or job with worst-cases execution time e i every p i time units. In addition, each task τ i provides two functions related to power-awareness. The function f i (t, s) defines the execution time of the task's instance requiring t time units at the processor speed level s, where t is the execution time at the maximum processor speed level. That is, a periodic job of τ i requires f i (e i , s) time units when the processor speed level is adjusted to s during its execution. Another function g i (t, s) defines the energy for executing t time units at the processor speed level s. Tasks have different f i and g i functions, because each task has different characteristics in terms of power-awareness.

div.head: B. Resource Model
div.p: A resource model specifies the amount of resource to be allocated to each component. In order to control the energy consumption of components, we propose a new resource model. The power-aware periodic resource model is defined as Γ(Π, Θ, Ψ), where Π > 0 represents the resource period, Θ is the resource allocation time per period (0 < Θ ≤ Π), and Ψ the relative speed level of resource supply. The poweraware periodic resource model Γ(Π, Θ, Ψ) guarantees periodic supplies of Θ times with a relative resource speed level of Ψ per Π time units.

While a component is provided with a periodic resource supply Γ(Π, Θ, Ψ), the local Dynamic Power Management (DPM) of the component can further adjust the processor speed level if necessary. This adjusted speed level is kept no more than Ψ.

div.head: C. Interface Model
div.p: In order to abstract the real-time requirements of a component together with its energy consumption, we propose the power-aware interface model that allows the component to be efficiently scheduled as a single task by the upper layer component. The power-aware interface model is defined by the quadruplet I(P, E, F, G), where P is the interface period and E the interface computational time for the resource period at the maximum resource speed level. In this interface model, F represents the execution time function under a given processor speed level, while G is the energy consumption function of the component task set for a given processor speed level. Thus, an upper-layer component can decide power-aware resource sharing for multiple sub-components based on their interface models.

div.head: D. Framework Overview
div.p: In a compositional scheduling framework, scheduling components are organized in a tree-like structure with parent component allocating resources to their child components. An overview of the proposed framework is given in Figure 1.

In Figure 1, component C 1 consists of two periodic tasks under the DVS-EDF (Dynamic Voltage Scaling Earliest Deadline First) scheduler. Interface I 1 is derived from the characteristics of C 1 . Similarly, interface I 2 is derived from component C 2 which have two periodic tasks under the Static-RM (Rate Monotonic) algorithm. These two interfaces are converted into corresponding tasks (τ 5 and τ 6 ) for the upper layer component C 0 . Now, component C 0 focuses on scheduling these two tasks without consideration of the two lower layer components. Indeed, component C 0 does not need to collect internal scheduling information such as the number of tasks and the scheduling policy about its child components. As a result of scheduling in C 0 , the power-aware periodic resource supplies R 1 and R 2 are allocated to its child components C 1 and C 2 , respectively. Thus, C 1 is provided 5 time units every 10 time units under the processor speed level 0.8. Similarly, 6 time units of resource is available to C 2 every 15 time units at the processor speed level 0.7.

div.head: III. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: The demand and supply bound analysis in [5] is used to analyze the feasibility of tasks in a component for a given a periodic resource model. If the demand bound of tasks is less than or equal to the supply bound of the resource model, tasks are guaranteed to be scheduled in their deadlines.

Let us assume that the processor slows down its speed level to Ψ during the execution of a component C. A new feasibility analysis is required with consideration of the speed level in our scheduling framework. This is done by deriving a new demand bound function for a given speed level.
For a power-aware periodic resource model Γ(Π, Θ, Ψ), the resource supply bound function which defines the minimum resource supply for any time interval t is defined by:
div.formula: sbf Γ (t) = ⎧ ⎨ ⎩ t -(k + 1)(Π -Θ) if t ∈ [(k + 1)Π -2Θ, (k + 1)Π -Θ], (k -1)Θ otherwise,(1)
div.p: where k = max( (t -(Π -Θ))/Π , 1) [5].

As the processor speed decreases, the resource demand of a task increases by f i (e i , Ψ) every period. Thus, we define the power-aware demand bound function pdbf W (A, t, s) as the worst-case resource demand of a task set W under the processor speed level s. The following two propositions provide the schedulability analysis under EDF and RM algorithms, respectively. The proofs are from Theorem 4.1 and 4.2 of [5] by replacing e i with f i (e i , Ψ) in dbf functions in [5].
div.formula: Proposition 1: A component C(W, R, A) is schedulable for a given resource R = Γ(Π, Θ, Ψ), where W = {τ i (p i , e i , f i , g i )} and A = EDF, if and only if, pdbf W (EDF, t, Ψ) = τi∈W t p i • f i (e i , Ψ) ≤ sbf Γ (t),
div.p: for all t such that 0 < t ≤ LCM W , where LCM W is the least common multiple of p i for all τ i ∈ W .
div.formula: Proposition 2: A component C(W, R, A) is schedulable for a given resource R = Γ(Π, Θ, Ψ) under the processor speed level Ψ, where W = {τ i (p i , e i , f i , g i )} and A = RM, if and only if, for all τ i ∈ W , there exists t ∈ [0, p i ] such that pdbf W (RM, t, Ψ, i) = f i (e i , s) + i-1 k=1 t p k • f k (e k , Ψ) ≤ sbf Γ (t),
div.p: where p 1 ≤ p 2 ≤ . . . ≤ p n in W . Example 3.1: Let us consider a component C 1 with two tasks, τ 1 (9, 1, f 1 , g 1 ) and τ 2 (15, 2, f 2 , g 2 ) for a given resource model Γ(5, 2, 1). The minimum resource supply of Γ, sbf Γ (t), and the resource demand bound function, pdbf W (EDF, t, 1), are shown in Figure 2. Since pdbf W (EDF, t, 1) of C 1 under EDF is always smaller than or equal to sbf Γ (t), as shown in Figure 2, two tasks of the component are guaranteed to meet their deadlines at the maximum processor speed.

Furthermore, the processor speed level can be reduced as there is a gap between pdbf W (EDF, t, 1) and sdb Γ (t) in Figure 2. This can be done by adjusting the speed level of the resource supply or by adjusting the speed level to increase the resource demand of tasks as shown in propositions 1 and 2. The execution time function of speed level of each task is assumed to be f i (t, s) = t/s. Let us assume that the processor speed level is adjusted into 0.8 during the component tasks execution. Figure 3 shows sbf Γ (t) and pdbf W (EDF, t, 0.8). Since pdbf W (EDF, t, 0.8) of C 1 under EDF is always smaller than or equal to sbf Γ (t), the processor speed level can be decreased by 0.8. The power-aware resource supply of the component can then be set as Γ(5, 2, 0.8).

However, in case of the speed level 0.6, there exist some points where pdbf W (EDF, t, 0.6) is greater than sbf Γ (t), as shown in Figure 4, which means that the speed level of 0.6 does not guarantee the schedulability of the two tasks. As the function g i (t, s) defines the energy requiring for executing t time units under the processor speed level s, the energy to execute one job of τ i is defined by g i (f i (e i , s), s). Thus, if a component is provided with periodic resource Γ(Π, Θ, Ψ), the energy for one periodic instance of task τ i is given by g i (f i (e i , Ψ), Ψ). The following proposition tells the total energy for executing the component under a given periodic resource model. Proposition 3: If a component C(W, R, A) is schedulable for a given resource R = Γ(Π, Θ, Ψ), the total energy in order to execute the component for LCM W is given by
div.formula: E C = τi∈W LCM W p i × g i (f i (e i , Ψ), Ψ),
div.p: where LCM W is the least common multiple of p i for all τ i ∈ W .

As shown in Figure 3, two tasks are schedulable at the processor speed level 0.8. The energy for executing one instance of τ 1 is given by 0.64 (=g 1 (f 1 (e 1 , 0.8), 0.8) = 1/0.8 • 0.8 3 ). Similarly, that of τ 2 is given by 1.28 (=g 2 (f 2 (e 2 , 0.8), 0.8) = 2/0.8 • 0.8 3 ). The total energy for 45 time units is 7.04 (=5 • 0.64 + 3 • 1.28). Thus, if the processor level is slow down to 0.8, the component C 1 is schedulable with less energy compared with the maximum speed level.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we proposed a new compositional scheduling framework for power-aware real-time systems. With the framework, we introduced the power-aware periodic resource model and the power-aware interface model. The schedulability analysis is provided not only for guaranteeing the realtime requirements of components, but also for minimizing their energy consumption. We are currently focusing on many interesting problems in the proposed framework, including global optimization in terms of energy, derivation of an optimal interface of a component, and development of an efficient power-aware scheduling of a component.
